That measure must first be constructed from interval lengths through a
measure extension theorem, with its existence proof and hypotheses
\cite[thms.~1.1.4, 1.1.9; app.~A.1]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
text:
The hypotheses are these. Theorem~1.1.4 assumes only that \(F\) is a
Stieltjes measure function, that is nondecreasing and right continuous,
and gives exactly one measure \(\mu\) on the Borel sets with
\(\mu((a,b])=F(b)-F(a)\) \cite[thm.~1.1.4, p.~3]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
Theorem~1.1.9 starts from a set function \(\mu\) on a semialgebra
\(\mathcal S\) with \(\mu(\varnothing)=0\) that is additive over finite
disjoint decompositions within \(\mathcal S\) and countably subadditive
over countable disjoint decompositions of a member of \(\mathcal S\) into
members of \(\mathcal S\); it then extends uniquely to a measure on the
generated algebra, and further to a measure on \(\sigma(\mathcal S)\),
uniquely when the extension to the algebra is sigma-finite
\cite[thm.~1.1.9, p.~5]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}.
All of these results are proved in \cref{sec:p15-measure-extension}:
the extension from a semialgebra to its algebra
(\cref{thm:p15-semialgebra-extension}), the existence of an extension
from an algebra to the generated sigma-algebra and its uniqueness under
sigma-finiteness (\cref{thm:p15-premeasure-extension}), the measure of a
Stieltjes function (\cref{thm:p15-stieltjes-construction}), Lebesgue
measure and the uniform probability space
(\cref{thm:p15-lebesgue-unit-interval}), and the existence of a law with
any admissible cumulative function
(\cref{thm:p15-cdf-existence}).
Durrett's construction of measures on \(\mathbb R^d\) from a function of
\(d\) variables \cite[thm.~1.1.11, ex.~1.1.12, pp.~6--9]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019},
including a counterexample to his Theorem~1.1.11 as printed, is treated in
\cref{sec:p15-w02c-p15-002-rd-measures}.
His remark that the quantile scheme of Theorem~1.2.2 generates
random variables from a uniform one \cite[p.~11]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}
is stated and proved in \cref{thm:p15-w02c-p15-002-inverse-sampling}, and
his justification of the distribution-function criterion for equality in
distribution by Theorem~1.1.4 \cite[pp.~11--12]{DurrettPTEAuthor2019}
in \cref{thm:p15-w02c-p15-002-equal-in-distribution}.

It contains \(\mathbb R\), is closed under complements by subtraction
from one, and under countable disjoint unions by the pointwise
sum of measure values. It is a lambda-system containing the
half-line pi-system, so contains every Borel set.
text:
It is a lambda-system in the sense of \cref{def:p15-pi-lambda}; each
defining condition is checked directly. First, \(\nu_\omega(\mathbb R)=1\)
for every \(\omega\), a constant function, so \(\mathbb R\) belongs to the
class. Second, let \(A\subseteq B\) be members. Each \(\nu_\omega\) is a
probability measure, so
\(\nu_\omega(B\setminus A)=\nu_\omega(B)-\nu_\omega(A)\), a difference of
two real measurable functions of \(\omega\); hence \(B\setminus A\) is a
member. Third, let members \(B_k\) increase to \(B\). Continuity from below
of each \(\nu_\omega\) gives \(\nu_\omega(B)=\lim_k\nu_\omega(B_k)\), a
pointwise limit of measurable functions; hence \(B\) is a member. The
half-lines \((-\infty,t]\) form a pi-system, since two of them intersect
in the one with the smaller endpoint, and they generate the Borel sets.
By \cref{thm:p15-measure-uniqueness} the class contains every Borel set.

It too is a lambda-system in the sense of \cref{def:p15-pi-lambda}.
For \(A=\mathbb R\) both sides equal \(P(B)\), since \(\nu_\omega(\mathbb R)=1\)
and \(W\) is real. Next, let \(A\subseteq A'\) be members. The values of
\(\nu_\omega\) lie in \([0,1]\), so all integrals below are finite, and
\(\{W\in A\}\subseteq\{W\in A'\}\); hence, for every \(B\in\mathcal G\),
\[
 \int_B\nu_\omega(A'\setminus A)\,dP(\omega)
   =\int_B\nu_\omega(A')\,dP-\int_B\nu_\omega(A)\,dP
   =P(B\cap\{W\in A'\})-P(B\cap\{W\in A\})
   =P(B\cap\{W\in A'\setminus A\}).
\]
Finally, let members \(A_k\) increase to \(A\). Then
\(\nu_\omega(A_k)\uparrow\nu_\omega(A)\) at every \(\omega\) by continuity
from below, so monotone convergence gives
\(\int_B\nu_\omega(A_k)\,dP\to\int_B\nu_\omega(A)\,dP\); and
\(B\cap\{W\in A_k\}\) increase to \(B\cap\{W\in A\}\), so
\(P(B\cap\{W\in A_k\})\to P(B\cap\{W\in A\})\). The two sequences are equal
term by term, so the limits agree and \(A\) is a member.

The class of Borel \(B\) for which \(\nu_Y(B)\) has that
conditional version property is a lambda-system, by the
whole-space, complement and disjoint-sum calculations from the
real-law proof. Rational half-lines generate, so the property
holds for every real Borel set.
text:
Let \(\mathcal L\) be the class of Borel \(B\) for which \(\nu_Y(B)\) is a
version of \(P(W\in B\mid\sigma(Y))\), that is,
\(E(\nu_Y(B)\mathbf1_G)=P(G\cap\{W\in B\})\) for every \(G\in\sigma(Y)\);
the random variable \(\nu_Y(B)\) is \(\sigma(Y)\)-measurable because
\(y\mapsto\nu_y(B)\) is \(\mathcal T\)-measurable. \(\mathcal L\) is a
lambda-system in the sense of \cref{def:p15-pi-lambda}, by the three checks
of the real-law proof with \(\nu_Y\) in place of \(\nu_\omega\): for
\(B=\mathbb R\) both sides equal \(P(G)\); for members \(B\subseteq B'\),
subtracting the finite values for \(B\) from those for \(B'\) gives the
identity for \(B'\setminus B\); and for members increasing to \(B\),
monotone convergence on the left and continuity from below of \(P\) on the
right carry the identity to \(B\). The rational half-lines lie in
\(\mathcal L\), form a pi-system and generate the Borel sets, so
\cref{thm:p15-measure-uniqueness} puts every real Borel set in
\(\mathcal L\).

It contains the whole space and is closed under complements by
subtraction from one. For disjoint \(E_n\), their sections are
disjoint and the value on their union is
\(\sum_nK(y,(E_n)_y)\), a measurable increasing sum.
Thus \(\mathcal D\) is a lambda-system containing the generating
rectangle pi-system, and includes every product measurable set.
text:
It is a lambda-system in the sense of \cref{def:p15-pi-lambda}. It
contains \(T\times S\), since \(K(y,S)=1\) for every \(y\). For members
\(E\subseteq E'\), the sections satisfy \(E_y\subseteq E'_y\) and
\((E'\setminus E)_y=E'_y\setminus E_y\), so
\(K(y,(E'\setminus E)_y)=K(y,E'_y)-K(y,E_y)\), a difference of real
measurable functions; and \(E'\setminus E\) is product measurable. For
members \(E_k\) increasing to \(E\), the sections \((E_k)_y\) increase to
\(E_y\), and continuity from below of \(K(y,\cdot)\) gives
\(K(y,E_y)=\lim_kK(y,(E_k)_y)\), a pointwise limit of measurable
functions. The rectangles form a pi-system, since
\((B\times A)\cap(B'\times A')=(B\cap B')\times(A\cap A')\), and they
generate the product sigma-algebra. By \cref{thm:p15-measure-uniqueness},
\(\mathcal D\) includes every product measurable set.
